title: Closing the Window on Wonder
author: Christopher Perrin
summary: Christopher Perrin begins with the marvel of powered flight and an odd observation from his own travels: on daylight flights most passengers keep the window shade down and watch screens instead. He uses the closed airplane window as a metaphor for how wonder has been shut out of modern life and, above all, of modern education. Wonder, he says, is the stimulus of curiosity and the engine of sustained learning, and progressive education pulled down one window after another through methods that treated teaching as engineering rather than art. He lists what students are missing, including the wonder of mathematics as puzzle and proof, literature and history as studies of the human heart, grammar, logic and rhetoric as liberating arts, and the study of the cosmos as wisdom. He argues the mistaken analogy between machines and children explains why the progressive project went down while believing it soared. The good news, he says, is a fifty-year return to traditional, liberal and classical education, and the piece ends with his publisher's new tagline, Wonder to Wisdom.
points: Perrin argues that wonder is the fuel of curiosity and sustained learning, and that modern schooling and screens have closed the window on it.
He faults progressive education for the mistaken analogy that if humans can engineer flight, education can be engineered, when teaching remains an art because children are not machines.
He names concrete losses: mathematics as play and proof, literature and history as studies of the human heart, the trivium arts, and the cosmos as a source of wisdom.
The traditional, liberal and classical tradition is presented as what reopens those windows, a return he says has been underway for about fifty years.
The airplane anecdote ties the argument to screens, since even good videos on an iPad keep a child from the sky outside the glass.
quotes: We have closed the window to wonder nearly everywhere. Wonder is the great stimulus of curiosity and the engine of sustained learning. We might say it is fuel for flight.

How ironic then it is to see children on a plane next to a closed window watching videos on an iPad–even good videos (I regard that as rare). What about the transparent glass right next to them opening to the earth and sky?
The slow advent and conquest of progressive, modern education has occurred as window after window has been pulled down.
The wonder of mathematics as puzzle, proof, and play–eternal, invisible, immaterial realities understood by symbols we employ–is largely unknown by students.
The study of grammar, logic, and rhetoric as arts that liberate the tongue to interpret accurately, reason precisely, and persuade eloquently–these are known to precious few.
But it was a mistaken analogy because education remains an art precisely because humans are not very much like cars or flying machines.
We call it by many names: traditional education, liberal (i.e. liberating) education, liberal arts education, classical education.
